lesson.title: Polling America: Building a Confidence Interval for One Proportion
lesson.summary: A one-proportion confidence interval uses a sample proportion, its standard error, and a critical z-value to estimate an unknown population proportion within a margin of error.
lesson.body:
Pollsters can never ask every voter, every customer, or every patient in a population, so they take a sample instead and use the sample proportion, p-hat, as their best single guess about the true population proportion, p. But a single number, a point estimate, does not communicate how much that guess might be off. A confidence interval fixes that by wrapping a range of plausible values around p-hat, built from exactly the ingredients you have already met: the sample proportion, the standard error that describes how much p-hat bounces around from sample to sample, and a critical z-value that sets how much of that variability you want to account for.

The formula for a one-proportion z-interval is p-hat plus or minus z star times the standard error, where the standard error is the square root of p-hat times (1 minus p-hat), divided by n. Each piece has a job. The point estimate p-hat centers the interval where your data actually points. The standard error, sqrt(p-hat(1-p-hat)/n), measures the typical spread of the sampling distribution of p-hat, smaller samples and proportions near 0.5 produce more spread, larger samples and proportions near 0 or 1 produce less. The critical value z star comes from the standard normal curve and is chosen to match your desired confidence level, for example 1.96 for 95 percent confidence, because the sampling distribution of p-hat is approximately normal when sample size is large enough (a condition the next chapter checks in detail). Multiplying z star by the standard error gives the margin of error, the amount added and subtracted from p-hat to build the interval.

Here is a full worked example. Suppose a news organization surveys 400 registered voters and finds that 220 of them support a proposed ballot measure. The sample proportion is p-hat = 220/400 = 0.55. The standard error is sqrt(0.55 times 0.45 divided by 400) = sqrt(0.2475/400) = sqrt(0.00061875), which works out to about 0.0249. For a 95 percent confidence level, z star is 1.96, so the margin of error is 1.96 times 0.0249, which is about 0.0488. The confidence interval is therefore 0.55 minus 0.0488 to 0.55 plus 0.0488, or roughly 0.501 to 0.599. In percentage terms, the survey supports a plausible range of about 50.1 percent to 59.9 percent backing the measure.

Notice how each prerequisite concept shows up in that single calculation: the confidence interval framework gives the plus-or-minus structure, the sample proportion supplies the center, standard error supplies the spread, and the z critical value supplies the multiplier that turns spread into a margin of error at a chosen confidence level. Once you can compute this interval by hand, the next questions become when the formula is trustworthy, what the resulting numbers actually mean, and how to control the interval's width, all covered in the chapters that follow.
